title: Every case entry carries the defendant's full offence list, not its own offences

oracle.activityBoundary: every callActivity argument and return value crosses oracle/lib/boundary.js
oracle.determinismCheck: the case was run twice at clockPinIso and the two document arrays compared

edits: hearing: a second prosecution case inserted at index 1, cloned from prosecutionCases[0] so every field shape is real fixture data.

the clone keeps prosecutionCases[0].prosecutionCaseIdentifier verbatim EXCEPT prosecutionAuthorityReference, which becomes "TFL-SECOND-CASE" — the authority ids stay identical so both cases belong to TFL.
the clone keeps only defendants[0] (masterDefendantId 6647df67-a065-4d07-90ba-a8daa064ecc4, the same master defendant as case 1), with fresh id.

that defendant's single offence gets offenceCode "XX99999", orderIndex 7, offenceTitle "Second case offence" and a fresh id, so the two cases' offences are distinguishable. Its judicialResults are the fixture's, untouched.

digests.convention: sha256 of the written file bytes — `sha256sum <file>` reproduces each value exactly

nodeEvidence.what: `getOffenceMapper() { return new OffenceMapper(this.hearingJson, this.informantRegister, this.registerDefendant).build(); }` — no case or application argument is passed in.
the SAME zero-argument call is made once per case (:26) and once per application (:41), inside loops over the defendant's cases and applications.

build() loops over EVERY prosecutionCase belonging to the authority (`for (let prosecutionCase of this.hearing.prosecutionCases || [])`, filtered only by prosecutionAuthorityId at :17) and accumulates into one derivedOffences array.

`derivedOffence.originatingCaseUrn = this.deriveCaseUrn(prosecutionCase.prosecutionCaseIdentifier);` — the offence DOES carry the reference of the case it really came from. So the duplicated entries are self-contradictory: caseOrApplicationReference says one case, the nested offence's originatingCaseUrn says another.

assertion: The hearing gives TFL two prosecution cases (references TFL4359536 and TFL-SECOND-CASE) that share one master defendant, each case carrying one distinct offence (PS90010 orderIndex 1 in the first, XX99999 orderIndex 7 in the second). Assert EXACTLY, on the TFL document, for the defendant that appears on both cases: (1) prosecutionCasesOrApplications has exactly 2 entries, with caseOrApplicationReference "TFL4359536" then "TFL-SECOND-CASE" in that order; (2) BOTH entries have an `offences` array of length 2; (3) in BOTH entries the offences are [offenceCode PS90010 with originatingCaseUrn "TFL4359536", offenceCode XX99999 with originatingCaseUrn "TFL-SECOND-CASE"] — i.e. the entry whose caseOrApplicationReference is "TFL4359536" still contains the OTHER case's offence, and that offence still points back at the other case. Assert the contradiction explicitly and by name; a test that only checks "offences.size() == 2" would pass a correct implementation too and would pin nothing. D8 is priority-2 in the design register: scoping offences to their own case changes what prosecuting authorities receive and needs a business decision plus a DEVIATIONS.md entry. A Java OffenceMapper that takes a caseId — the obvious, tidy design — produces one offence per entry and MUST fail this test until that decision is recorded.
